label: Homogeneous Coordinates
notes: This chapter, printed pages 47 through 66, rebuilds the plane from three coordinates. The single idea to carry through is that a point is no longer a pair but a ray through the origin in three-space, and that this one move erases the exceptional cases that plague ordinary coordinate geometry.

label: Points as Rays
notes: Stress that a homogeneous point is the whole nonzero scalar class, not any one representative. Scaling a triple by a nonzero lambda changes the representative but not the point. The ray picture in three-space is the mental model students should keep returning to all chapter.

label: The Affine Chart w=1
notes: The plane w equals one is just a screen that most rays pierce exactly once. Reading a finite point means dividing by w. Emphasise that the chart is a view of the projective plane, never the whole thing, so different charts reveal different points cleanly.

label: Points at Infinity
notes: Rays lying flat in the plane w equals zero never reach the chart, so they record directions rather than locations. Walk through the limit: moving farther along p plus alpha r sends the affine point to infinity while the rescaled homogeneous vector converges to the direction triple.

label: Lines as Triples
notes: A line is also a nonzero triple, read as a plane normal or covector. Incidence is the single symmetric equation a x plus b y plus c w equals zero. Point that this is literally the dot product vanishing, the first hint of the point-line symmetry developed next.

label: Point-Line Duality
notes: Points and lines live in algebraically identical spaces and incidence treats them symmetrically. Therefore any theorem phrased only with point, line, incidence, join, and meet has a valid dual obtained by swapping those words. This is the structural payoff of the homogeneous model, not a coincidence.

label: Join and Meet by Cross Product
notes: The cross product does double duty. The join of two points is their cross product, a vector orthogonal to both, hence the line through them. Dually the meet of two lines is again a cross product. One operation, read two ways, captures both incidence constructions.

label: Parallels Meet at Infinity
notes: Run the worked example: two affine lines that look parallel have a meet whose w coordinate is zero. The same cross-product formula returns a finite intersection or a point at infinity with no special casing. This is the concrete reward for the homogeneous bookkeeping.

label: Projective Transformations
notes: A projectivity is an invertible three by three matrix taken up to scale, acting on point representatives by left multiplication. Make clear that scalar multiples of the matrix give the same map, mirroring how scalar multiples of a triple give the same point.

label: Lines Transform Contravariantly
notes: To keep incidence true under a map M, lines cannot transform the same way as points. They transform by the inverse transpose, since M-inverse-transpose l dotted with M p equals l dot p. Walk through that one-line algebra; it justifies the contravariant rule completely.

label: Finite Projective Planes
notes: The same recipe works over a finite field GF of q. Normalise nonzero triples modulo scalars for both points and lines, and declare incidence by the dot product vanishing mod q. The count q squared plus q plus one and the unique-line property fall out automatically.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the three moves: points and lines are rays, incidence is one dot product, joins and meets are one cross product. Remind students the line at infinity is a choice, not intrinsic, and that this coordinate machinery powers the projective transformations and conics studied next.
